1:
Where the chapter joins on is disputed, and Barnes lays the options out. The ancient Greek expositors and Grotius took the previous chapter's picture of Paul keeping his own body under as the hinge, so that the Corinthians are warned not to be lulled by the gifts conferred on them; Macknight treated the chapter as an independent handling of three questions submitted to Paul; Barnes himself judges the connection to be with the eighth chapter. Ellicott agrees, tracing the thread back to the offer there to forgo a right, from which the writer was led aside. Robertson settles a small point: the correct reading is for, not but, so that Israel's experience confirms what Paul has just said of himself, the peril being real and not imaginary. Calvin describes the temper addressed, the Corinthians taking their ease at the very outset of the course as though they had served out their time and been honourably discharged.

The privileges are then set beside our own. Calvin denies any difference of condition that would blunt the comparison: they enjoyed the same benefits, and there was a Church of God among them as now among us. Henry puts it more memorably, that Judaism was Christianity under a veil, wrapped up in types and dark hints, the gospel preached to them in their legal rites and sacrifices; and he lingers on the cloud, which sometimes drew into a pillar shining on one side to show the way and dark on the other to hide them from pursuers, and sometimes spread over them as a sheet against the sun. Wesley states the warning bluntly, that they were God's elect and peculiar people and were nevertheless rejected. Gill lists what undid them, lust and fornication and intemperance and idolatry, so that their carcasses fell in the wilderness; and Clarke holds these circumstances of Jewish history typical of the greatest mysteries of the Gospel.

On the baptism unto Moses they agree that no rite was administered and divide on what the figure implies. Barnes insists the word carries two senses and that the second is meant: not the application of water by any man's hand, but dedicating, initiating, bringing under obligation, since passing under the cloud and through the sea publicly recognised them as followers bound to Moses's laws. Clarke says the same in a sentence, that they were baptized into the covenant of which Moses was mediator, as Christians are baptized into Christ. Ellicott finds the evidence favouring the middle voice, so that they voluntarily had themselves baptised to Moses, God's representative under the Law. Robertson reports the manuscript division between that causative middle and the passive, then presses the picture: the cloud over them and the walls of the sea on either side made the immersion complete. Wesley's guess runs the opposite way, that they were perhaps sprinkled here and there with drops from the sea or the cloud, by which baptism might be the more evidently signified.

Lightfoot supplies the Jewish background. He argues that circumcision had lapsed in Egypt, since the prophet charges them with conforming to Egyptian customs and idols (Ezekiel 20:7), and that God therefore provided by a special precept at the Passover that every one be circumcised before eating it, which he takes to be confirmed by the later statement that all who came out of Egypt were circumcised. To circumcision baptism was then added, in the cloud and in the sea; and the point he draws from the order is that the second seal did not take away the first but superinduced a new obligation. His sharpest observation is the difference of preposition: they were not circumcised into Moses, but they were baptized into Moses. He grants that the Jews themselves date their baptism from Sinai, but holds that the apostle fetches the thing higher.
3:
Why the manna is called spiritual is answered the same way by four hands and complicated by a fifth. Barnes takes the word to mean given directly by God and not produced in the ordinary way, and notes that the Psalm calls it angels' food and Josephus divine and extraordinary food. Ellicott contrasts bread from earth with bread from heaven. Clarke observes that the phrase is not Paul's but borrowed from the Jews, who called that bread spiritual and those waters spiritual; Gill confirms it from the same quarter while denying that the manna was spiritual in its own nature, being corporeal food that nourished the body. Calvin alone raises the difficulty: the Lord treats the manna as corruptible food of the belly and sets the true food of the soul against it, the opposite of what is claimed here.

His solution is a principle rather than a gloss. Scripture, he says, sometimes speaks of the sacraments according to the capacity of the hearers, having respect not to the nature of the thing but to the mistaken idea in their minds; Paul himself, he shows, varies his account of circumcision on the same ground. So the manna fed body and soul at once, and the Lord's words strip it only of the value his hearers put on it. Wesley points the type two ways, to Christ and to the bread eaten at his table.

The rock that followed is the harder question, and the answers separate. Lightfoot denies that the rock in Horeb moved and says the streams from it followed, gathering into pools wherever they encamped; he supports it from the prophetic figure of pools in the wilderness and from a Targum which has the well of Mattanah made into overflowing brooks that climbed the mountains and descended into the valleys. Clarke reaches the same conclusion by naming the device, rock put by metonymy for its water, though he grants there is no direct proof, and reports the older Jewish account of streams that followed up hills and down valleys and formed cisterns where they camped. Calvin dismisses as frivolous the objection that a rock standing firm could not follow, the grace being extolled in water commanded to flow wherever the people journeyed. Ellicott takes a different line: a tradition held that a fragment broken from the smitten rock travelled with them, and he judges that Paul adopts that account rather than the narrative in Numbers, as illustrating God's abiding presence better. Robertson knows the legend, in one form a rock fifteen feet high, and reports that Baur and others think Paul took it over, but finds that hard to believe and allows at most an allusion given a spiritual turn.

On the last clause the caution runs the other way. Calvin objects to those who make the rock spiritual in the sense of ceasing to be a visible sign, since the passage concerns outward signs, and presses the past tense as marking something peculiar to the fathers. Robertson finds the pre-existence of Christ stated here in symbolic form and quotes the warning that we must not disgrace Paul by making him say the pre-incarnate Christ followed the march as a lump of rock. Ellicott sets the dispensations side by side, God manifest in the Rock being the Christ of the older, and observes that the Jews knew God as a Rock poetically without seeing what it prefigured. Gill presses the striking, since the waters did not flow until the rod fell, as Christ was smitten by the rod of the law. Cyril uses the verse to prove that the one Moses saw was Christ, joining it to the request to be shown God's face: because no man could see the face of the Godhead and live, he took the face of human nature, and even that, shining to the measure of the disciples' capacity, threw them down affrighted.
5:
How many is many turns out to be contested. Barnes says it should have been rendered with most of them, literally with the many, so God was pleased with but few. Ellicott makes it sharper still, not the greater part but in fact all except two. Robertson calls it a mournful understatement, since only two reached the promised land, and expounds the verb for overthrow as laying a whole generation low, spread down like a couch, as if by a hurricane. Gill resists the arithmetic: whether they were the greater part is not certain, and the saved cannot be reduced to Joshua and Caleb, since Moses and Aaron and Miriam died in the wilderness too, and it is to be hoped thousands more who were not outside the grace of God. The apostle means those who were instances of divine vengeance.

The lesson drawn from it splits along familiar lines. Clarke takes the case as decisive: these people had every outward ordinance and shared the grace of Christ, and their fall proves that such may abuse their privileges, grieve the Spirit and perish everlastingly; he warns those who keep asserting this impossible that their own security may make them the proof, and recalls who first said men should not surely die. Calvin uses the same history for humility rather than for a doctrine of falling. He then raises a question the others do not: if hypocrites in that age ate spiritual meat, do unbelievers now partake of the reality in the sacraments? Some, fearing that man's unbelief would detract from God's truth, teach that the wicked receive the reality with the sign; the fear is needless, since the Lord genuinely offers to all what he represents, though not all can receive it.

On the word rendered examples the interest is philological and then structural. Robertson traces it from the verb to strike: first the mark of a blow, as of the print of the nails, then a pattern to be imitated or, as here, avoided, and at last a type in the doctrinal sense. Ellicott prefers types of us and hears a contrast between a physical Israel dying physically and a spiritual Israel that dies spiritually if privileges are abused. Barnes guards it the other way, that the events were not designed as types but held up as admonition. Calvin explains why he departs from the Vulgate and Erasmus here, their versions obscuring the point that God presented a picture in that people for our instruction. Wesley notices the arrangement: the benefits stand in Moses's order, the sins do not, evil desire coming first as the foundation of all, then idolatry, then fornication. Henry agrees on the reason, carnal appetites indulged being the root and source of much sin and gaining strength by indulgence, so they must be checked at their first rise.

The idolatry meant is the golden calf, and what the worshippers did after eating divides them. Barnes notes how apt the instance was, a feast in an idol's honour whose food was mainly the sacrifice itself. Clarke presses their logic, that those who offered thought the god fed invisibly with them, so that every guest communicated with it. On rising up to play he differs from the Jewish interpreters, who confine the word to idolatrous acts, holding that it covers the accompanying impurities as well as the dances. Calvin says the passage is rightly interpreted by few, most treating the meal as ordinary excess on the proverb that dancing follows a full diet, whereas Moses describes a sacred feast kept in the idol's honour. Robertson reads the imperative as stop becoming idolaters, implying some had already begun. Gill sees the same inclination in men who carried liberty as far as sitting in a temple; Wesley notes the exquisite propriety with which the person changes to the second here, Paul being himself in no danger of this sin.
8:
The three and twenty thousand set against Moses's four and twenty thousand draws five answers. Clarke harmonises by addition: the heads of the people were to be hanged, perhaps a thousand of them, and twenty-three thousand fell by the plague, which makes the larger figure; he notes two manuscripts with the later Syriac and Armenian reading twenty-four thousand here, but judges them too slender to disturb the text. Barnes offers a choice between that solution, which he takes from Grotius but with the thousand assigned to Phinehas and his companions, and Macknight's, that the true figure lay between the two and could be stated in round numbers either way; he concludes only that Paul has not exceeded the truth. Calvin needs no reconciliation, since it is usual, where heads are not being counted exactly, to put down a number that comes near. Ellicott declines the exercise: the point being historically unessential, the likeliest explanation is that the writer quoted a small fact from memory, or used a copy of the Greek version carrying these figures. Lightfoot, who reports that the Talmudists also give the larger number, allows that Scripture varies its reckonings when a story is told twice, citing Kings and Chronicles.

The next warning turns on a reading. Clarke acknowledges that several manuscripts have the Lord and a few God, but holds that Christ carries the greatest authority, and draws a conclusion: this is no mean proof that the person called Jehovah in the Old Testament is called Christ in the New. Robertson takes the opposite view, that the best manuscripts read the Lord, and observes that the compound verb is used in the New Testament only of Christ. Ellicott agrees on internal grounds and explains the third reading, God having probably begun as a marginal note to relieve the difficulty of saying that Israel tempted Christ.

What the tempting consists in is answered more evenly. Barnes distinguishes the senses of the word, since with men it means presenting inducements to sin and with God trying his patience to see how much he will bear, and supposes the Corinthians did it by making an experiment on the grace of Christ under the influence of idolatry. Gill says the same of men who presume on Christ's power to keep them and sit down to meat in an idol's temple to see whether he will preserve them. Calvin locates the root further back, in impatience: the people could not wait for the time God appointed, and the evil is wishing to go before him and bind him to our own inclination. Wesley notices a symmetry, five benefits set down and five sins, with Christ named expressly in the fifth benefit as the fourth sin is committed against him.

Which murmuring is meant is disputed, and Calvin argues it. Barnes takes it of the people disappointed at being led into a wilderness, complaining of their leaders and proposing to return to Egypt, and Wesley cites the same chapter. Calvin rejects that view, since the spies' disheartening report was punished by no sudden chastisement but only by exclusion from the land, whereas the words here describe another kind of stroke; he refers it instead to what followed the punishment of Korah. Ellicott and Robertson read it the same way, Ellicott adding that the murmuring was against God-given leaders, which is the point of the parallel with the Corinthians and their apostle. On the destroyer they converge. Ellicott finds it notable that the death is ascribed to a messenger where the older narrative says plague, every pestilence being such a messenger; Robertson says the noun occurs nowhere else and points to the destroying angel of the Passover; Lightfoot presses it hardest, distinguishing the Jewish classes of destroying and ministering angels, asking where the people were ever slain by an evil angel, and concluding that the allusion is to the angel of death.
11:
Two of them warn against over-reading the purpose clause. Barnes denies that the events took place solely to be examples, holding that they illustrated standing principles of human weakness and divine government and could therefore serve later generations; Ellicott makes the same distinction and adds that the verb for what happened is plural, covering the several occurrences, while the verb for what was written is singular and refers to the record itself. Calvin is content with the plain sense, that these are lively pictures showing God angry at such sins, and prefers it because it stops the mouths of men who wrest the passage to make that people's whole history nothing but figure. On the ends of the ages Clarke takes the times bounded by the Mosaic economy, and reports another writer's parallel that its beginning and end match, both lasting forty years, both filled with temptation and unbelief, both closing in the destruction of unbelievers. Robertson reads the plural as marking how one stage succeeds another in human history, and Wesley presses its force, that benefits and dangers alike come to a crisis under the last dispensation, with only the coming of Christ as avenger left.

On the warning that follows, Clarke and Wesley make the same lexical point independently: the verb rendered thinketh is used by the best writers to strengthen the sense rather than weaken it, so that the man addressed is the one who stands most confidently, sure his heart is right. Barnes turns it into a rule, that confidence in one's security is no evidence of safety and may be among the strongest evidences of danger, the safest being those who feel their weakness. Gill names the same self-trust, in a man's own strength or in his gifts. Ellicott points at Corinth, where murmuring against apostolic teachers and the wish to go as far in indulgence as one could without actual sin were significant symptoms. Calvin agrees that no one may glory in his beginnings or progress so as to fall asleep in confidence, but blocks a use made of the verse in his own day, that faith must always carry doubt with it, distinguishing two kinds of assurance.

Whether the next verse consoles or rebukes is genuinely open. Chrysostom reads it as a check on pride: having terrified them with the ancient examples, and knowing they might answer that they were no strangers to trouble, having been driven and persecuted, the apostle tells them their temptation is only such as man can bear, which he glosses as small, brief and moderate. Clarke adopts that gloss by name, their trials being trifling beside Israel's and easily resisted. Gill reports the reproachful reading as one option, since they had not yet resisted unto blood. Calvin states the alternatives and chooses: others think the apostle chides their cowardice in yielding under so slight a trial, but for his part he takes the verse as consolation, lest men hearing such instances of wrath should be overpowered and despair of repentance.

The last clause is read for practical comfort. Ellicott makes God's permission and God's care two halves of one act, since he allows the circumstances that create the temptation but sees that no fate bars the road back, and calls the verse perhaps the clearest exposition anywhere of free will in relation to God's overruling power. Wesley renders the disputed adjective as proportioned to human strength and rests the promise on God's faithfulness. Robertson notes that the noun for the way out is rare, and that this exit stands alongside the temptation from the first, so that yielding is both cowardice and distrust. Clarke says it most vividly: Satan is never permitted to block the way without providence making a passage through the wall, breaching what would otherwise be an impregnable fortification.
14:
The command to flee is read as urgent by most and as easy by one. Ellicott hears affection in the address, the warning given not because they were enemies but because they were beloved, and turns the imperative into a rule: do not try how near you can get to idolatry, but how far from it. Barnes joins it to the promise just made, since Paul had told them God was faithful yet did not expect God to keep them without effort of their own, so they must escape the feasts and the temples alike. Wesley says it in six words, from idolatry and from all approaches to it. Clarke alone makes light of it, calling this a trial of no great magnitude which a moderate portion of grace and circumspection is enough to escape. Calvin defines the offence: he does not suspect the Corinthians of worshipping idols in their hearts, but of making no scruple about frequenting the assemblies of the wicked and observing the rites kept there, and that is what stands condemned.

The appeal to their judgment is taken by some at face value and by others as veiled rebuke. Robertson states plainly that there is no sarcasm here, only a plea that they use the mind given them, and Ellicott insists the words are not hypothetical but express the standing from which they are addressed, as men competent to feel an argument. Henry draws a principle from it, that it is no dishonour to an inspired teacher, and no disadvantage to his case, to refer its truth to the reason and consciences of his hearers, since it then comes upon them with the greater force. Clarke turns it round: the Corinthians valued themselves on their wisdom, and the apostle admits the claim to draw an argument from it against them. Calvin finds a tacit reproof too, that men accurately instructed in the school of Christ allowed themselves a gross vice about which there was no difficulty in forming an opinion.

The cup is explained from the Jewish table. Gill traces the title to the cup taken at common meals and at the passover, over which God was blessed and thanked and which bore that very name; Clarke derives it likewise from the passover cup. Ellicott notices what nobody else does, that the cup is named here before the bread and elsewhere after it, and reports two explanations, one from heathen feasts where the libation preceded the food, the other that the writer means to dwell longer on the bread. He draws a further inference from the plural: the one who presides consecrates as representing the whole company, not as a man individually possessed of some miraculous gift. Calvin fixes on the verb and refuses the easier sense: to bless is not simply to give thanks, whatever the word may mean elsewhere, since the construction will not bear it, and the proposal to supply a preposition he judges exceedingly forced. To bless the cup is to set it apart, that it may be to us an emblem of the blood of Christ.

What the partaking amounts to is then stated with care. Robertson takes the noun rendered communion from the word for a partner, notes that it can also mean fellowship or a contribution, and settles it as a spiritual participation in the blood which the cup symbolises. Clarke draws the comparison that governs the argument, that those who partake of the cup have fellowship with Christ exactly as those at an idol feast participate, so far as they can, with the idol. Wesley words it more cautiously, calling cup and bread the means of partaking of the benefits purchased by the blood and body of Christ. Barnes sets out the chain the chapter will follow, from the believer's dedication in the communion to Israel devoted by the altar and the heathen sacrificing to demons.
17:
Clarke and Ellicott both reverse the English word order to recover the argument: because there is one loaf, we the many are one body. Clarke supports it from the passover, where a single loaf was used and those who shared it counted as one body. Ellicott presses the mechanics: the one bread is broken up, each receives only a fragment, yet all partake of what was one. Barnes denies that the phrase is a remark about numbers, since the many means all, and finds the point in the loaf made of separate grains, eating together being a token of unity in almost every nation. Gill uses the same figure of grains ground into one, Robertson identifies the body as Christ's mystical body, Wesley the communion itself as the bond. Calvin says love is not his design here but mentions it in passing, and adds a warning: Scripture often names one part of the Supper for the whole, so it is a foolish cavil to argue from the bread alone that the people were meant to be deprived of the cup.

The Israel appealed to next is qualified, and everyone marks it. Gill sets the phrase against the spiritual Israel of God and calls those meant carnal men in a carnal worship; Barnes and Clarke take it of Jews not converted, Clarke naming Christians Israel after the Spirit; Robertson divides the literal people from a spiritual Israel of Jews and Gentiles. Ellicott corrects the English rendering: the sacrifice was divided, part burnt and part eaten, so the eater became a partaker in common with the altar, not of it, and Robertson agrees. Calvin adds what the law required, that only a man duly prepared might eat, so all who ate shared in the sanctification by which God set apart his Temple; and if the ancient figures held so much virtue, we must reckon on more in our own Supper.

The question that follows is read two ways. Clarke takes it as a Jewish idiom for I conclude, and gives the conclusion: since the Gentiles sacrifice to demons, those who partake have fellowship with demons, and no professing Christian can hold fellowship with Christ and the devil at once. Barnes hears instead a self-interrogation in the present tense, and observes that the Corinthians had themselves been quoted as saying an idol is nothing; Paul does not contradict them, but his reasoning has brought their attendance into question, so he raises the matter by question rather than assertion. Ellicott states the objection anticipated, that the preceding verse might seem to grant the heathen offerings as much reality as Israel's altar, which he had earlier denied. Calvin puts the difficulty more bluntly, that the apostle may seem to argue inconclusively or to allow idols some power, and answers that he looks not at the idols but at the intention of those who sacrifice, where the pollution lies; he grants that an idol is nothing.

What the demons are is then disputed. Ellicott takes the word plainly of evil spirits, the heathen world lying under the dominion of the Evil Spirit and his emissaries. Barnes shows that the heathen used it either well or ill, of spirits inferior to the supreme God, genii or attending divinities, some good and some evil, instancing the genius Socrates supposed to attend him; he also notes the omitted but understood negative, an ellipsis after a question familiar in classical writers and in Scripture. Robertson traces the phrase to the Greek of Deuteronomy, takes not to God to mean to a no-god, and reads the argument as a reply to the heathen claim that the god represented was worshipped and not the wood or stone. Calvin supplies the understood negative himself, insisting that the work must be estimated by the impious intention behind it, since no one sits down at an idol feast but declares himself a worshipper.
21:
The impossibility asserted is moral, and two say so. Barnes calls it a striking instance of cannot used for moral rather than natural inability, since they plainly had the physical power; Robertson says the same. Gill puts it as a matter of truth rather than permission, since no one can really drink the one cup in the faith of Christ's sacrifice while drinking the other to a heathen deity. Clarke turns it on the professors, that it is vain to profess Christ while frequenting these festivals, and documents the pagan practice from a passage of Virgil, the very passage Barnes cites here. Robertson notes that the word for table means what is on it, and that the altar of burnt offering bears that name in the prophets; Lightfoot confirms it, the table of the Most High being a usual phrase among the Talmudists for the altar. Wesley reduces it to one clause, that a man cannot have communion with both.

The rebuke that follows is unusually sharp. Calvin explains the change of tone: a most atrocious offence was treated as a trivial error, and the Corinthians wanted their liberty reckoned excusable, as none of us willingly allows himself to be found fault with but seeks one subterfuge after another; to argue so is to wage war against God, who requires nothing more than that we hold strictly to his word. Robertson identifies the verb as the one used in the song of Moses of the old Israelites' insolence, and Barnes connects it with the declaration that God is jealous. Clarke supplies the figure that makes the word intelligible, idolatry being a spiritual adultery in which the heart covenanted to God is given to Satan, and reads the second question as an appeal to omnipotence. Wesley sharpens it into a phrase, whether we provoke him by caressing his rivals; Gill says only that he admits no rival in worship.

The maxim of liberty is then quoted back and qualified. Ellicott explains the structure, that the writer is closing the question he had branched off from, and limits the principle by two tests, an act's effect on ourselves and its influence on the Church. Henry states the caution as a rule, that a man must consider not barely what is lawful but what is expedient and will edify, even in private conduct. Barnes puts it more strongly: the reasons making a lawful thing inexpedient ought to have the binding force of law. Calvin does not dispute the lawfulness, replying only that regard must be had to edification, and Robertson notes that building up is offered as the explanation of expediency. Clarke makes it personal, that eating all kinds would not become him, offending and grieving many weak minds. Gill secures the ground first, that no creature is common or unclean in itself, then adds three limits: not as sacrificed, not in a temple, not before a weak brother.

How far the rule against seeking one's own extends is disputed. Clarke states it without reserve, that a man live not for himself but for every part of the great human family around him. Robertson makes it Paul's standing rule for social relations, rendering the second clause as the affair of the other man. The others narrow it. Barnes holds that though the injunction takes a general form it should be read of the matter in hand, a man being able to forgo these things without injury but not to indulge without endangering others. Calvin denies that individuals are forbidden to consult their own advantage, requiring only that they be willing to give up part of their right when a brother's welfare needs it. Gill says plainly that a man may lawfully seek his own good, temporal, spiritual and eternal. Ellicott ends on a word, observing that the English wealth once meant good and especially moral welfare, and has narrowed since to temporal possessions.
25:
Chrysostom explains why the permission comes here. Having led them from the idol tables by every argument and filled them with great fear, the writer had to keep that fear from driving them to the other extreme, alarmed lest something forbidden reach them unawares from the market; the permission releases them, and he adds that a man who eats in ignorance is not liable, the matter being one of ignorance and not greed. Barnes and Ellicott give the reason: having been offered cannot change the quality of the meat, and once in the public market it is simply meat, bought as meat and not as sacrifice, so the advice does not contradict what went before. Clarke divides the victim three ways: one part burnt on the altar, a second eaten by the sacrificer, which he forbids absolutely, and a third falling to the priest and often sold in the market. Robertson notes that the word for market is transliterated Latin found only here, and quotes the picture of poor Christians buying their modest pound of meat in the market at Corinth, as vivid as the excavated one at Pompeii.

Two of them turn to the Jewish parallel and the Psalm. Lightfoot reports that the rabbis debated a similar question, how far one might buy meat from a heathen when it might be torn, and preserves the retort that one man's indecency was no reason to forbid every market; the Jews, he adds, were vexed with innumerable scruples about what they ate, with whom, and how. Robertson observes that the verse was a common grace before meat. Calvin asks what the quotation has to do with the argument and answers that possession of the whole earth stays in God's hands, and what he holds he preserves and sanctifies. Barnes puts it negatively, that the food never belonged to the idol and its nature is unchanged; Clarke says nothing God made can be impure; Ellicott adds that only meat regarded as an actual sacrifice could be reckoned of devils; Gill grounds the freedom in Christ's breaking down the middle wall; Wesley reads the earth's produce as given to men without scruple.

On accepting a heathen's invitation the tone divides. Barnes is expansive: this is a private house and not a temple, the going is plainly allowed, the Saviour accepted such invitations, and Christianity does not abolish the courtesies of social life or make men misanthropes and hermits. Robertson agrees, distinguishing a general banquet from a temple feast and saying the guest should behave like a gentleman. Calvin will not go so far. He reads the wording as an indirect signal that the writer does not altogether approve and would rather they declined, nothing being better than keeping clear of such snares; but because the thing is indifferent he will not forbid it outright.

The exception turns on who speaks. Barnes argues that the informant must be a fellow guest, since a host would hardly point out food on his own table whose lawfulness he doubted. Gill leaves both open, a weak believer heading off what he thinks a sin or the unbeliever testing his guest to draw him into a snare. Ellicott notices what the informant is made to say: the term here for meat offered to an idol is not the condemnatory word used elsewhere, which he explains by courtesy, a Christian at a heathen's table choosing an epithet that would not offend his host. He also states the danger, that a weak brother who has just shown he thinks the thing wrong may be led by the other's example to eat and so defile his conscience, which is Wesley's point too. Clarke adds a textual note, that the clause about the earth being the Lord's, repeated here in the received text, is absent from a long list of manuscripts, versions and fathers and has been dropped by an editor.
29:
The question about liberty being judged by another conscience looks like a reversal, and Barnes says so, that as it stands it seems to contradict what has just been urged, and reports that Macknight and others read it as an objection raised against the apostle. Ellicott agrees, treating it as a querulous objector's complaint about the restriction just imposed, answered not narrowly but by the principles that follow. Robertson has the writer step into the place of the strong brother, expected to conform his conscience to the weak brother's; two individualities clash, and the one reason for yielding is love, in what he calls the eternal collision between progress and reaction. The others take the sentence straight. Clarke denies that the Gospel lays any man under a general burden of doing nothing at which a weak brother might be hurt, gospel liberty not taking the scrupulosity of any conscience for its rule. Calvin says the same with a distinction: bear with a brother's weak conscience so as not to offend, but never let the restraint on outward use entangle your own.

The following question is read as a matter of prudence. Barnes glosses the opening as partaking by grace and asks why court censure over eating when so many bounties of providence are open without it. Robertson makes the calculation explicit, whether the risk of being evil spoken of is worth one's liberty, and adds that saying grace over food one should not eat looks inconsistent. Calvin narrows the blame: we cannot stop the wicked reviling us or the weak being displeased, but the reproof falls on those who volunteer occasions of offence when neither necessity nor expediency requires it. Gill takes the grace as either Christian liberty or the creatures God has given.

The rule that closes the argument is universal, and they press its reach. Calvin holds that no part of life and no action so minute is exempt from being directed to God's glory. Ellicott goes furthest, denying that the modern division of acts into religious and secular is recognised anywhere in Paul: no act is in itself either, the quality of each depending on the spirit that guides it and the motive it springs from, so a religious act done in a secular spirit is secular and a secular thing done in a religious spirit is religious. Wesley reaches the same by enumeration, things religious and civil alike, common actions with sacred, all bent on advancing the knowledge and love of God first in one's own soul and then in all mankind. Barnes notes that God's glory here means his honour; Robertson calls it the ruling motive of a Christian's life rather than having one's own way; Clarke finds in it a sufficient rule for every indifferent thing on which there is no express command; Gill applies it to ordinary meals, where every mercy is owned as from God.

The last two verses are qualified as soon as stated. Ellicott makes giving no offence the practical test of the rule just laid down, the sphere now reaching beyond the Church to Jew and Greek alike; Calvin says we are debtors to all, even strangers; Barnes explains why each party needs its own care, the Jews abhorring the least approach to idol worship and the Gentiles seeking countenance for theirs. Then the limits appear. Wesley adds the condition, if and as far as it is possible. Gill excepts an incumbent duty, such as the pure preaching of the Gospel, not to be avoided though men take offence. Calvin warns that some stretch the example to unlawful things, as though one might go farther for a neighbour than the Lord permits, whereas the accommodation was in things indifferent only, nothing against men's salvation being conceded. Ellicott corrects the last clause, the profit sought being that of the whole mass of men, not merely of a great number.
